posts.text:
Introducing GPT‑6 Cyber: a major advance in security research that pairs stronger capabilities with better model alignment.

The model powered the Linux kernel research we announced yesterday, and security teams at companies like Mozilla, Palo Alto Networks, Calif, and Cisco—alongside our own at OpenAI—are already putting it to work.

GPT-6 Cyber is available to select Daybreak Red customers and we are expanding access over time.
posts.why_viral: First major public reveal of a specialized cyber model tied to real-world kernel patching results.
posts.why_it_matters: New capability for automated vulnerability discovery and patching available to select defenders, with clear expansion path.

posts.text:
Our security researchers built an autonomous cyber vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and patching pipeline.

In a single run with an upcoming cyber model, it validated and generated patches for 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel at a total API cost of $1.2 million.
posts.why_viral: Concrete numbers on scale (948 vulns) and cost ($1.2M) for autonomous AI-driven security work.
posts.why_it_matters: Demonstrates practical cost and throughput of AI for large-scale software security work that builders can benchmark against.

posts.text:
New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models.

Here, we introduce FlashProve. Building on established cryptographic techniques, FlashProve allows developers to verify whether a given response came from a given AI model. It’s substantially more efficient than prior open-source methods for doing so. 

These proofs have a range of applications. They can, for instance, make it harder for attackers to hijack a chat, or enable safety evaluators to verify that the model they’re testing is the same one being served to customers.

For our full write-up, see here: https://t.co/OIZWPb6QZa

Further progress in provable inference will likely be an important part of improving trust in AI deployment. To that end, we're open-sourcing FlashProve’s code, here: https://t.co/7ky3Ir8V06

We’re grateful to our collaborators: Alessandro Chiesa, @GiacomoFenzi, @gwberg95, @miranda__christ, Rahul Dalal (https://t.co/pjWKLHWXyz) and Ben Mayer (@transmissions11).
posts.why_viral: Open-source tool for cryptographic verification of model outputs with clear security use cases.
posts.why_it_matters: Developers can now more efficiently prove that a response came from a specific model, improving trust and safety checks.

posts.text:
We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more:
posts.why_viral: Concrete example of AI accelerating a real scientific structure determination from weeks to days.
posts.why_it_matters: Shows practical speedups and limitations when using frontier models on complex scientific workflows.

posts.text:
New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor.

These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior.

Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute.

Read the full post on the Alignment Science Blog:
posts.why_viral: Novel automated red-teaming approach that generated subtle misalignment examples at scale.
posts.why_it_matters: Provides a path to more scalable safety testing for anyone building or evaluating agents.

posts.text:
As AI becomes more capable at finding vulnerabilities, defenders need to put it to work before attackers do.

We’re planning our next internal security sprint at OpenAI and partnering with Cathedral Systems, whose researchers will use our models alongside our teams to challenge our defenses. They’ll bring differentiated expertise and approaches to our ongoing work to find and fix weaknesses with AI.

We’re also raising bug bounty rewards, including more than quadrupling rewards for critical findings. Exceptional findings will be eligible for up to $172,000, including bonuses.

We’ll keep advancing our models, using them to strengthen our own systems, and expanding access for trusted defenders.
posts.why_viral: Significant increase in bug bounty payouts tied to AI security capabilities.
posts.why_it_matters: Higher incentives and clearer defender access for teams using AI to harden systems.

posts.text:
We asked Mistral Large 4 to show what happens when you break a molecule. ⚛️

With a short prompt, it wrote a quantum chemistry SCF solver from scratch, validated its output, and built a 3D view around it. 

Le Chonk also understand chemistry enough to independently choose how to break the molecule and what orbitals to show, without further input. 🧵
posts.why_viral: Short-prompt demonstration of an open model generating and validating scientific code end-to-end.
posts.why_it_matters: Shows current open-weight models can produce working scientific tooling from minimal instructions.

posts.text:
We built PlanAssist to help UK Government planning officers speed up building and renovations across the country.

Built with Gemini, it has shown it can cut the time planning officers spend assessing householder applications by up to 58%. It is now being made available to 12 more councils to help them to make faster decisions. 🏡 →
posts.why_viral: Real-world government deployment with a quantified 58% time reduction.
posts.why_it_matters: Concrete example of agentic workflows delivering measurable efficiency gains in regulated processes.

posts.text:
Friday was my last day at Anthropic.

Two years ago, when Claude Code was a small internal tool, I asked it to build an RL env. I steered it for tens of hours but never manually wrote a line of code. It worked, I was hooked, and I joined the team.

When we first launched, most people approved every permission prompt by hand and mostly used Claude to answer questions and write tests. 

Today, the default is trusting Claude's judgment to auto-approve. Claude does large migrations and builds new products. 

Helping build Claude Code into an industry-defining product has been the journey of a lifetime. 

Thank you to the incredible team behind Claude Code, Cowork, and Tag. These products are the sum of thousands of great ideas from you. I'll miss working with you all.

Thank you to our users for embracing a new way of working. Your constant feedback shaped so much of what we shipped and your stories made the work so meaningful.

Excited to see what you all make next!
posts.why_viral: Insider retrospective on the rapid shift from manual approval to autonomous coding agents.
posts.why_it_matters: First-hand view of how production agent usage evolved from cautious Q&A to large-scale code generation and migration.

posts.why_it_matters: Actionable details on how to improve agent memory and error correction in production systems.

posts.text:
running a company nowadays feels kinda dystopian

my team is 50+ people in 12 countries, but i talk to my agents more than my human teammates

- voice note to grokbot
- mattpocock/skills /grill-me so the agent interrogates the idea before anything gets built
- spec drops into linear through the linear mcp
- exa + firecrawl agent reads every competitor site, pricing page and changelog
- https://t.co/a5ARFnvSnA to find ideas and trends
- apify pulls g2, reddit and app store reviews
- prompt: "find the 10 complaints that show up most and quote the users"
- context7 so the agent reads the latest docs before it touches any api

the design

- claude code + paper mcp
- 4 versions of every screen before a single line of code
- pick pieces from 2, it merges them. diverge then converge
- frontend-design skill from anthropic/skills + our own design system skill
- cleanshot screenshots of any ui i like go straight in with "make it feel like this"

the build

- pingdotgg/t3code as the control surface for every agent, from my phone too
- stablyai/orca runs a fleet of agents in parallel, each in its own git worktree
- graphify maps the whole codebase into a knowledge graph so agents navigate instead of guess
- headroom compresses tool outputs before they hit the model, so tokens go 20-95% further
- lsp plugins so the agent sees types and errors like an ide does
- security guidance hook flags risky edits before they land
- supabase mcp for the database, stripe for billing
- github mcp opens the pr, vercel spins up a preview
- loops run overnight, i check what shipped over coffee

the user testing

- lightpanda as the headless browser, way lighter than chromium so you can run hundreds at once
- agents click every flow on the preview like a first-time user
- one persona is impatient, one is confused, one is on a phone
- playwright + chrome devtools mcp for regression tests

the bugs

- sentry mcp catches the error
- agent reads the stack trace and opens a fix pr in under 10 minutes
- human just approves

the data

- posthog mcp cron at 7am on yesterday's funnel
- any step that drops more than 10%, the agent watches 20 session replays and tells me why
- stripe mcp pulls every cancellation reason into one doc every monday

the agents' tools

- orgo so every agent gets its own computer
- agentmail so every agent gets its own inbox
- agentphone so i can call them from the car
- composio connect-apps for every other connector
- akitaonrails/ai-memory, a git-backed markdown wiki so they remember what we decided last week

the skills

- wshobson/agents so skills work across claude code, codex and opencode
- my writing voice
- our design system
- how we write specs
- skill creator so the agents write new skills themselves

some helpful tricks

- one agent per platform. the x agent never touches email
- cheap model for triage, opus for anything that ships
- every output gets scored 1-10 by an llm judge. under 8 goes back
- every agent writes a 5-line log at night so i can read the whole company in 2 minutes
- every agent mistake becomes a new skill, so it only happens once

the team

- humans get version 5, not my voice note which they are happy about lol 
- their job is creative feedback, relationships and telling the agents what they got wrong

a human pm reviews the funnel once a week. this reviews it every morning

running a company is now voice notes and inference
posts.why_viral: Detailed, concrete stack for running an entire company primarily through agents.
posts.why_it_matters: End-to-end practical architecture (tools, skills, evaluation loops, overnight runs) that founders can adapt immediately.

posts.text:
If you learn AI Security Engineering, you will never be unemployed again.

I’ll do this.

Stage 1: AI Attack Surfaces & Threat Modeling
- Learn:  OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, STRIDE for AI, the "Confused Deputy" problem in agentic workflows & data flow mapping.

- Practice:  Draw a complete threat model for an AI agent that reads emails and writes to a CRM, identifying every indirect injection and data exfiltration vector.

- Why:  You cannot secure an agentic workflow if you don't understand how an attacker can hijack the agent's legitimate privileges.

Stage 2: Advanced Prompt Injection & Jailbreaking
- Learn:  Direct vs. Indirect injection, Crescendo attacks (multi-turn grooming), payload splitting and encoding evasion (Base64, ROT13).

- Practice:  Build an automated harness that successfully bypasses a commercial LLM's system prompt using a multi-turn Crescendo strategy.

- Why:  Basic "ignore previous instructions" filters are trivial to bypass. Modern attacks groom the model's context over multiple turns.

Stage 3: Agentic Security & MCP Tool Poisoning
- Learn:  Model Context Protocol (MCP) security, JSON-RPC sanitization, shadow tool execution and least-privilege scoping for agents.

- Practice:  Write an MCP server that strictly validates incoming tool parameters via Pydantic and blocks "confused deputy" attacks where a user prompt tries to access admin tools.

- Why:  Agents are only as secure as the tools they call. Tool poisoning is the SQL Injection of the Agentic Era.

Stage 4: RAG Security & Data Poisoning
- Learn:  Vector DB access control, citation spoofing, shadow context injection and row-level security for semantic search.

- Practice:  Inject a "poisoned" document into a RAG pipeline that forces the LLM to output a specific malicious URL when queried about company policy.

- Why:  If an attacker can slip a poisoned document into your knowledge base, they own every answer the AI generates.

Stage 5: PII, Privacy & Cryptographic Guardrails
- Learn:  Deterministic masking, UUID swapping, differential privacy and pre-flight/post-flight unmasking proxies.

- Practice:  Build a middleware proxy that intercepts user prompts, swaps SSNs and credit cards for UUIDs before the LLM sees them and restores them post-generation.

- Why:  Compliance teams will kill any AI product that sends raw customer PII to a third-party frontier API.

Stage 6: Identity, Auth & Delegated Access for Agents
- Learn:  OAuth2 for machine identities, scoped JWTs, human-in-the-loop (HITL) approval gates and agent-to-agent (A2A) trust boundaries.

- Practice:  Build an auth broker where an AI agent acts on a user's behalf using a heavily scoped, time-limited OAuth token, rather than holding the user's raw password.

- Why:  Agents need hands but they should never hold the master keys to the enterprise.

Stage 7: Output Validation & Grammar-Constrained Guardrails
- Learn:  CFG (Context-Free Grammar) decoding, NeMo Guardrails, output sanitization and regex-enforced JSON schemas.

- Practice:  Implement a guardrail layer that physically prevents the LLM from generating markdown links or executable code blocks in its final output.

- Why:  You cannot rely on the system prompt to "please don't output bad things." You must enforce it at the token-decoding level.

Stage 8: Automated Red Teaming & Fuzzing
- Learn:  Microsoft PyRIT, Garak, LLM-based fuzzing, adversarial dataset generation and CI/CD security gates.

- Practice:  Build a CI pipeline using PyRIT that automatically attacks your agent with 1,000 adversarial payloads on every PR, blocking merges if the jailbreak rate exceeds 1%.

- Why:  Manual red teaming doesn't scale. You need automated, continuous adversarial fuzzing integrated directly into your deployment pipeline.

Stage 9: Model Extraction & IP Protection
- Learn:  Membership inference attacks, model inversion, API rate-limiting by semantic similarity and output watermarking.

- Practice:  Build an API gateway that detects and blocks scraping bots trying to extract your fine-tuned model's weights via thousands of systematic, low-temperature queries.

- Why:  Your fine-tuned model's weights are your IP. Competitors will try to distill your model through the public API.

Stage 10: Mechanistic Interpretability & Alignment Safety
- Learn:  Activation patching, logit lens, circuit discovery, detecting reward hacking and tools like TransformerLens.

- Practice:  Locate the specific attention heads in an open-source model responsible for "deception" or "sycophancy" and patch their activations to neutralize the behavior.

- Why:  You cannot fix hidden biases or misalignment if you treat the neural network as a black box. 

Stage 11: Compliance, Auditing & Governance
- Learn:  EU AI Act requirements, NIST AI RMF, immutable audit trails, SOC2 for AI and bias testing frameworks.

- Practice:  Build an immutable, append-only audit log that records the exact prompt, retrieved context, tool calls and final output for every single agent action.

- Why:  When an AI agent makes a mistake that causes financial or legal damage, the enterprise must be able to prove exactly why it happened.

Stage 12: Public CVEs, Teardowns & Portfolios
- Learn:  Responsible disclosure, writing security advisories, publishing threat models and bug bounty hunting for AI.

- Practice:  Find a vulnerability in an open-source AI framework (like LangChain or an MCP server), responsibly disclose it and publish a teardown of the exploit chain.

- Why: AI Security is a brand new field. Publishing novel attack vectors and defenses makes you the undisputed authority in the space.

Bookmark and Repost!
posts.why_viral: Comprehensive, staged curriculum with concrete practice exercises for AI security.
posts.why_it_matters: Actionable learning path covering prompt injection, MCP poisoning, RAG attacks, and governance that teams can implement now.

posts.text:
i reverse engineered wispr flow, then used deepseek to fine-tune LFM3-1.7B. the result is on par with the wispr flow models you pay for, and it's free, open source and runs entirely on your mac.

key-up latency is 65 ms on my m4 max vs ~520 ms for wispr flow on the same clips. a 6 minute yap session pacing around my office still lands in about a quarter second.

> rust backend with a native metal engine: each decode step runs as one fused megakernel
> a dflash2 speculative drafter is built into the engine, trained on my local 4 x rtx pro 6000 server
> parakeet transcribes, LFM3-1.7B refines. both stream while you talk, so key-up only waits on the last chunk
> never leaves your macbook, so slow internet or bad ping is no longer an issue
> import your own dictionary of terms for your workflow
> i picked every default myself. it feels amazing out of the box
> adapts to the app you're in: discord is lowercase casual, slack and email are formal, claude code gets clear prompts
> training data: 77k transcripts of public audio and synthetic dictations, each rewritten by deepseek v4.1 flash 1017 following a written spec of what "what you meant" means, in 4 writing modes. none of my own dictations went into it
> blind judge (claude opus) on an hour of lectures: phonon's text preferred 90 times, wispr's 23
> built with claude opus 5.5 [xhigh]

brew install --cask infatoshi/tap/phonon
posts.why_viral: Specific latency numbers and open-source path that beats a paid product on local hardware.
posts.why_it_matters: Replicable recipe for fine-tuning a small model into a production-quality local dictation tool with measured gains.
